title: edge-node-disk-inode-starvation-incident-notes
body:
Summary:
During a midnight maintenance window (UTC), an edge cluster experienced rapid inode exhaustion on three nodes in the us-west-2-edge pool. The inode pressure caused kubelet to be unable to create new container dirs, which cascaded into failed pod starts, CNI (calico) failures for new pods, and a scheduling backlog that looked like a partial cluster outage for a subset of customer traffic routed to the edge tier.

Impact:
- Duration: ~00:18 to ~02:10 UTC (partial recovery by autoscaler/proactive draining actions).
- Affected customers: 2% of traffic for real-time inference routes served from us-west-2-edge (spikes in 95th percentile latency and error rates).
- Control plane: etcd and API server remained healthy; control-plane metrics didn’t show sustained errors.
- Symptoms: Pod create failures (OOM/ENOSPC-like messages), CNI errors during endpoint creation, and nodes entering NotReady after kubelet failed to manage local housekeeping.

Timeline (reconstructed):
- 00:02 UTC: Scheduled cronjob (log-collector-rotate) triggered a pre-shipped cleanup that created many tiny files under /var/lib/log-collector/tmp on edge nodes A, B, C.
- 00:08 UTC: Node-level inode usage increased rapidly on nodes A/B/C; kubelet started throwing errors when creating ephemeral container directories: "open /var/lib/kubelet/pods/...: no space left on device" with ENOSPC mapped to inodes.
- 00:10 UTC: First PagerDuty alert: pod creation failure rate up by +400% for edge pool. Pager metadata indicated multiple nodes reporting similar disk/inode errors.
- 00:12 UTC: SRE on-call (Riley) joined incident channel; initial triage confirmed inode saturation, not block device full.
- 00:20 UTC: Attempts to restart kubelet failed to allow new pods to be scheduled; existing pods remained running but health checks sporadic due to CNI.
- 00:33 UTC: Calico failed to program endpoints for newly scheduled pods; errors in calico-node logs: "failed to create endpoint: write /var/run/calico/ep-*: no space left on device".
- 00:45 UTC: We tainted nodes A/B/C with node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable=true to prevent further pod placement pending cleanup.
- 01:05 UTC: Runbook action: freed inodes by removing /var/lib/log-collector/tmp/* and rotated some leftover application debug logs. Nodes reported freed inodes and kubelet regained ability to create directories.
- 01:20 UTC: Calico agent recovered state; endpoints reprogrammed. New pod starts resumed but backlog persisted on scheduler.
- 02:05 UTC: Autoscaler + manual reschedules reduced backlog; traffic normalized approx 02:10 UTC. Post-incident monitoring run for 48h.

Key findings:
1) Root cause: a log-rotation change in log-collector cron generated a very large number of tiny temp files (inodes) that were not GC'd promptly. The system had sufficient raw block space but exhausted inodes on the root filesystem (/).
2) Kubelet and Calico both assume the ability to create local runtime files (container dirs, sockets). Inode exhaustion causes both control-plane interactions (CNI programming) and local kubelet failures, which manifest as pod creation errors and intermittent network setup failures.
3) Etcd and apiserver were not the bottleneck; controller loops were backing off because kubelet reported transient errors, not because of API errors.
4) Node eviction/tainting and taint propagation prevented further scheduling but existing traffic on surviving nodes still suffered elevated latency while CNI recovered.

Commands and diagnostics used:
- ssh node and: df -i / | awk '{print $5, $6}'  # inode usage
- sudo find /var/lib/log-collector/tmp -type f | wc -l  # confirm file count spike
- journalctl -u kubelet -n 500 --no-pager | grep -i ENOSPC
- kubectl describe node <node>  # see allocatable and conditions
- kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp | tail -n 200  # surface pod creation failures
- kubectl logs -n kube-system calico-node-<id>  # check CNI errors

Mitigations performed (real-time):
- Tainted nodes A/B/C to stop scheduling new pods (prevented further failures while remediation proceeded).
- Manual inode cleanup: rm -rf /var/lib/log-collector/tmp/* and incremental deletion of stale debug files under /opt/app/debug-dumps.
- Restarted calico-node and kubelet only after inode usage dropped to <70% to avoid restarting into the same failure window.
- Temporarily increased pod replica counts on healthy nodes (reschedule to non-edge pool where latency acceptable) via scale policies and manual overrides for the busiest services.

Shortcomings of current runbook discovered:
- Runbook assumes ENOSPC equates to block-level disk full; no quick checklist to detect inode exhaustion specifically.
- No automatic alert for inode percentage; only block usage alarms existed.
- No preflight for cronjobs that create many files in /var/lib; absence of per-cron inode quotas or better tmp cleanup.
- CNI recovery steps were generic (restart pod) but we lacked a safe order-of-operations to prevent endpoint duplication or transient blackholing during mass restarts.

Immediate post-incident action items (P0/P1):
- P0: Add inode-based alerting on nodes (alert when inode usage > 85% for 3m) and correlate with inode-creating cronjobs. Owner: Maya. Due: 2025-09-15.
- P0: Update runbook with explicit ENOSPC diagnostic checklist (df -i, find counts, identify common paths). Owner: Riley. Due: 2025-09-13.
- P1: Add cleanup step to the log-collector cronjob to GC temp files older than 2h; add integration test that creates many temp files and ensures GC runs. Owner: DevOps (PR linked). Due: 2025-09-20.
- P1: Establish safe CNI recovery order: drain node, cleanup inodes, restart calico-node, restart kubelet, verify endpoints. Formalize in runbook. Owner: Ethan. Due: 2025-09-17.
- P2: Evaluate per-node inode quotas or move tmp directories to a separate partition with more inodes and quota enforcement. Owner: Infra. Due: 2025-10-01.

Longer-term (backlog):
- Partition strategy: move ephemeral heavy directories (/var/lib/log-collector/tmp, /var/log/debug-dumps) to a partition with higher inode density and monitor.
- Work with platform engineering to add inode-aware scheduling signals to the autoscaler (avoid rescheduling heavy filesystem workloads to nodes with high inode usage).
- Add chaos test that simulates high small-file creation to ensure monitoring + runbook actions work under load.

Open questions / unresolved items:
- Why were temp files not cleaned by the log-collector's own GC? (investigating edge-case where rotation lock conflicts prevented GC runs).
- Should we add automatic cronjob throttling if inode usage is high? Risk: a cronjob that backs off might leave stale partial files. Need design review.
- Confirm whether other clusters share the same log-collector config; run inventory.

Lessons learned (for runbook and team practice):
- Always check inodes (df -i) when seeing ENOSPC or noisy file-system related kubelet errors.
- Distinguish block-full vs inode-full in alerts and runbooks. Small files are common with debug/logging agents and create a unique failure mode.
- Tainting nodes early prevented further scheduling mistakes, but we need a checklist for recovering CNI state to avoid prolonged network blackholes.
- Prefer separating ephemeral high-churn paths onto dedicated partitions or tmpfs where appropriate.

Appendix: useful snippets and pastebins
- Quick inode check: df -i --output=ipcent,target | awk 'NR==2{print $1}'
- Count by path: for p in /var/lib/* /var/log/*; do echo $p $(sudo find $p -type f | wc -l); done | sort -k2 -n | tail -n 10
- journal snippet (example): "kubelet[1234]: E0911 00:09:57.123456 12345 kubelet.go:234] failed to create pod log dir: open /var/lib/kubelet/pods/abcd/volumes: no space left on device"
- Calico error example: "level=error msg="failed to create endpoint" error="write /var/run/calico/ep-xyz: no space left on device""

Post-incident review meeting notes scheduled:
- Time: 2025-09-19 16:00 UTC
- Attendees: SRE on-call rotation, DevOps, Infra, Calico owner, Product-ops representative
- Objectives: validate P0/P1 tasks, review root-cause for gc failure, and agree on partition/quotas approach.

If you're reading this as a runbook draft: please add any missing commands you used, update the owner fields if you take an action item, and attach logs or relevant jenkins/github run ids to the linked_artifacts field above.

-- Riley
(On-call, eng-sre)
